content: Miconazole injection is no longer available in the United States. If you are currently using this medication, you should contact your doctor to discuss alternative treatments. Your doctor has prescribed miconazole, an antifungal antibiotic, to treat your infection. This medication will be administered intravenously, meaning it will be added to a fluid that drips through a needle or catheter placed in your vein. The infusion will take 30 to 60 minutes or longer, depending on your prescribed dose, and will be given three times a day. Miconazole is used to treat various infections, including those affecting the lungs, blood, and skin. In some cases, it may be prescribed for other conditions. If you have questions about its use, consult your doctor or pharmacist. Your healthcare provider will monitor the effectiveness of the treatment and any potential side effects through laboratory tests and physical examinations. It is essential to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. The duration of your treatment will depend on how your infection and symptoms respond to the medication. Before starting miconazole, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to miconazole or any other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription drugs you are taking, including antibiotics and vitamins. Let your doctor know if you have a history of liver or gastrointestinal diseases, particularly colitis. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while using miconazole, contact your doctor immediately. Before administering miconazole, inspect the solution carefully. It should be clear and free of any floating particles. Check the bag or container for leaks by gently squeezing it or observing it closely. Do not use the solution if it is discolored, contains particles, or if the bag or container is leaking. Instead, use a new solution and show the damaged one to your healthcare provider. Follow your healthcare provider’s instructions precisely when using this medication. Do not stop your treatment without consulting your doctor, as this could worsen your infection and potentially lead to hospitalization. Do not alter your dosing schedule without approval from your healthcare provider. If you encounter a mechanical issue, such as a blockage in the tubing, needle, or catheter, your healthcare provider may instruct you to stop the infusion. Miconazole may cause side effects. Notify your healthcare provider if you experience any of the following symptoms, especially if they are severe or persistent: upset stomach, vomiting, diarrhea, fever, drowsiness, decreased appetite, anxiety, blurred vision, dry eyes, headache, or a bitter taste in your mouth. Some side effects may be serious. Contact your healthcare provider immediately if you experience any of the following: pain, swelling, warmth, or redness at the injection site; rash; itching; unusual bleeding or bruising; irregular heartbeat; facial swelling; or difficulty breathing. If you experience a severe side effect, you or your doctor may report it to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. If you are receiving miconazole intravenously, your healthcare provider will likely supply you with several days’ worth of medication at a time. Store the medication at room temperature as directed. Keep your supplies in a clean, dry place and out of reach of children. Your healthcare provider will instruct you on how to safely dispose of used needles, syringes, tubing, and containers to prevent accidental injury. In the event of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. If you are receiving miconazole through a vein or under the skin, be aware of the signs of a catheter-related infection. Notify your healthcare provider immediately if you experience tenderness, warmth, irritation, drainage, redness, swelling, or pain near the site where the needle enters your vein or skin. Miconazole is sold under the following brand names: Micatin®, Monistat-Derm®, and Zeasorb-AF®.
